name: Kanada
dates_notes: Dating is anchored only by the relative position of the Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra to the Nyāya-Sūtra and to the early Buddhist Abhidharma; Frauwallner places Kaṇāda in the late centuries BCE, Halbfass in the first century BCE to first century CE. The biographical figure is a name attached to a sūtra-text; nothing personal is reliably known.

lineage_polemical.note: Brahma-Sūtra 2.2.11–17 refutes the Vaiśeṣika paramāṇu-kāraṇa-vāda — the doctrine that atoms are the world-cause — through the structural impossibility of unconscious atoms initiating the first conjunction (saṃyoga) at creation.

Brahma-Sūtra-Bhāṣya 2.2.11–17 develops Bādarāyaṇa's refutation: Śaṅkara argues that paramāṇus, being acetana, cannot self-initiate conjunction; a conscious cause is required, contrary to Vaiśeṣika atheism.

Madhva is unusual among Vedāntins in redeploying Vaiśeṣika categories positively — viśeṣas are central to his ontology of internal differentiation within otherwise-identical entities (svagata-bheda); the relation is constructive on padārtha-theory, polemical on atomistic cosmology.

core_thesis: Kaṇāda is the traditional author of the *Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra*, a foundational text of Vaiśeṣika realism. It analyzes reality through the categories of substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity, and inherence; later tradition adds absence. The school’s account of ultimate particularity explains the distinctness of eternal substances, including atoms. Composite physical things are explained through atoms of earth, water, fire, and air, while space, time, direction, and selves are non-atomic substances. The text connects causal processes to *adṛṣṭa*, the unseen moral residue of action, and describes liberation as release from the qualities that constitute embodied experience. The *Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra* does not clearly formulate the later theistic system. Its categorial framework was developed by Praśastapāda and integrated with Nyāya in subsequent philosophical traditions.

engaged_works.title: Vaisesika-Sutra
engaged_works.composition_dates_notes: Composition fixed only by the text's relative position to the Nyāya-Sūtra and early Abhidharma.
engaged_works.ascription_notes: Uniformly ascribed to Kaṇāda (also Kāśyapa, Ulūka) by tradition; the composite-text question — whether the surviving sūtras are a single redaction or a layered compilation — remains open in modern scholarship.

ascription_evidence.description: Frauwallner (Geschichte der indischen Philosophie II); Halbfass (1992, On Being and What There Is); Matilal (Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika).

engaged_works.summary: Ten *adhyāyas*, each in two *āhnikas*, of compressed *sūtras*. The first *adhyāya* ([VS 1.1.1–4](cite://ramanuja/vedartha-samgraha/1.1.1-4)) states the six *padārthas* and gives the school's account of *dharma* as the means to *abhyudaya* (worldly flourishing) and *niḥśreyasa* (the highest good) ([VS 1.1.2](cite://ramanuja/vedartha-samgraha/1.1.2)). The second and third *adhyāyas* ([VS 2.1–3.2](cite://ramanuja/vedartha-samgraha/2.1-3.2)) analyze *dravyas* — earth, water, fire, air, *ākāśa*, *kāla*, *dik*, *ātman*, *manas* — and establish the inferences for the supersensible substances (*ātman* from desire and aversion at [VS 3.2.4](cite://ramanuja/vedartha-samgraha/3.2.4); *manas* from the impossibility of multiple simultaneous cognitions at [VS 3.2.1–3](cite://ramanuja/vedartha-samgraha/3.2.1-3)). The fourth and fifth *adhyāyas* ([VS 4.1–5.2](cite://ramanuja/vedartha-samgraha/4.1-5.2)) analyze *guṇa* and *karma*. The sixth *adhyāya* ([VS 6.1–6.2](cite://ramanuja/vedartha-samgraha/6.1-6.2)) gives the school's ethics — *dharma* as Vedic *codanā*-conformity supplemented by *abhyudaya*-promoting acts. The seventh *adhyāya* ([VS 7.1–7.2](cite://ramanuja/vedartha-samgraha/7.1-7.2)) analyzes *sāmānya*, *viśeṣa*, and *samavāya* (esp. [VS 7.2.26–31](cite://ramanuja/vedartha-samgraha/7.2.26-31)). The eighth and ninth *adhyāyas* ([VS 8.1–9.2](cite://ramanuja/vedartha-samgraha/8.1-9.2)) analyze cognition and the *vidyās*, including the doctrine of *yogi-pratyakṣa* ([VS 9.1.11–15](cite://ramanuja/vedartha-samgraha/9.1.11-15)). The tenth *adhyāya* ([VS 10.1–10.2](cite://ramanuja/vedartha-samgraha/10.1-10.2)) analyzes pleasure, pain, and the *mokṣa*-doctrine: cessation of the nine *viśeṣa-guṇas* of *ātman* ([VS 10.2.9](cite://ramanuja/vedartha-samgraha/10.2.9)). The text is unintelligible without commentary; the principal classical commentaries are Candrānanda's *Vṛtti* and Praśastapāda's later, recasting *Padārtha-Dharma-Saṅgraha*.
